facts.claim: The wind chill in °F, from the air temperature T in °F and the wind V in mph at 10 m: 35.74 + 0.6215 T − 35.75 V^0.16 + 0.4275 T V^0.16. It's defined at 50 °F (10 °C) or colder with a wind above 3 mph (5 km/h), and assumes no sun.

source.title: US National Weather Service: Understanding Wind Chill

versions.note: Its chart, in °C and km/h: −30 °C in a 50 km/h wind feels like −49.

source.title: Environment and Climate Change Canada: Wind chill and the Wind Chill Index → How to estimate the wind chill

facts.claim: The same wind chill index in °C, as Canada and the United States have used it since 2001, from the air temperature T in °C and the wind V in km/h at 10 m: 13.12 + 0.6215 T − 11.37 V^0.16 + 0.3965 T V^0.16. It starts from this many degrees.

versions.note: C = 13.12 + 0.6215 T − 11.37 V^0.16 + 0.3965 T V^0.16, for T in °C and V, the wind at 10 m (the standard anemometer height), in km/h; the constants correlate it to the wind at 1.5 m, a face's height.

facts.claim: The body keeps its core temperature at or near this.

versions.note: The human body attempts to maintain a core temperature at or near 37 °C. Section: Physiology of hypothermia.

source.title: Dow et al. 2019, Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update (Wilderness Environ Med 30(4S), S47–S69)

facts.claim: Mild hypothermia is a core of this: the climber is conscious and shivering, and their movement is impaired.

versions.note: Mild at 35 to 32 °C; thermoregulatory shivering functional, increasing as the core cools. Swiss HT I: clear consciousness with shivering.

source.title: Dow et al. 2019, Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update (Wilderness Environ Med 30(4S), S47–S69)

versions.note: Mild: movement impaired, shivering, alert and conscious.

source.title: American Family Physician 102(9), 571–572 (2020): Accidental Hypothermia: Guidelines from the Wilderness Medical Society

versions.note: Conscious; shivering. Intense shivering first, then impaired movement; lethargy and clumsiness.

source.title: MSD Manual Professional Edition: Hypothermia (Danzl, reviewed August 2026)

facts.claim: Moderate hypothermia is a core of this: consciousness falls and shivering slows or stops, and the body can't rewarm itself any more.

versions.note: Below 32 °C thermoregulation becomes less effective, rewarming is possible only with exogenous heat, and consciousness decreases. Swiss HT II: impaired consciousness without shivering.

source.title: Dow et al. 2019, Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update (Wilderness Environ Med 30(4S), S47–S69)

versions.note: Moderate: movement impaired, shivering slows or stops, not alert, still conscious.

source.title: American Family Physician 102(9), 571–572 (2020): Accidental Hypothermia: Guidelines from the Wilderness Medical Society

versions.note: Impaired consciousness; shivering absent; confusion follows lethargy and clumsiness.

source.title: MSD Manual Professional Edition: Hypothermia (Danzl, reviewed August 2026)

facts.claim: Severe hypothermia is a core of this: the climber is unconscious and doesn't shiver, and the heart is at risk.

versions.note: Severe below 28 °C: most patients unconscious and not shivering, the risk of VF or asystole high. Swiss HT III: unconscious, 28 to 24 °C.

source.title: Dow et al. 2019, Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update (Wilderness Environ Med 30(4S), S47–S69)

versions.note: Unconscious.

source.title: MSD Manual Professional Edition: Hypothermia (Danzl, reviewed August 2026)

facts.claim: Profound hypothermia is a core below this: the chance of survival is much lower, the heart likely to stop.

versions.note: Profound hypothermia at <24 °C or <20 °C; the chance of survival appears much lower, probably because of a high likelihood of cardiac arrest. Swiss HT IV, apparent death: 24 to 13.7 °C.

source.title: Dow et al. 2019, Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update (Wilderness Environ Med 30(4S), S47–S69)

versions.note: Profound, under 24 °C: apparent death.

source.title: MSD Manual Professional Edition: Hypothermia (Danzl, reviewed August 2026)

facts.claim: Vigorous shivering can raise a cold-stressed or mildly hypothermic climber's core by this much an hour, if they're insulated well enough to keep the heat.

versions.note: Shivering can raise core temperature by 3 to 4 °C·h⁻¹; the patient must be adequately insulated to retain the heat. Section: Shivering.

source.title: Dow et al. 2019, Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update (Wilderness Environ Med 30(4S), S47–S69)

facts.claim: Rewarming in the field, insulated and with outside heat, warms a hypothermic patient by this much an hour, the safe rate.

versions.note: The rewarming methods described achieve the safe rewarming rate of 1 to 2 °C·h⁻¹. Section: Field rewarming.

source.title: Dow et al. 2019, Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update (Wilderness Environ Med 30(4S), S47–S69)

facts.claim: Below a core of 32 °C the body can't rewarm itself: it needs heat from outside.

versions.note: Below 32 °C (moderate hypothermia), thermoregulation becomes less effective and rewarming is possible only with addition of exogenous heat.

source.title: Dow et al. 2019, Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update (Wilderness Environ Med 30(4S), S47–S69)

versions.note: Thermoregulation ceases below approximately 30 °C; the body must then depend on an external heat source for rewarming.

source.title: MSD Manual Professional Edition: Hypothermia (Danzl, reviewed August 2026)

facts.claim: Exercise and shivering raise the body's heat enough to prevent hypothermia, so long as the climber has eaten enough and is insulated well enough; beyond that, clothing and shelter prevent it.

versions.note: Exercise and shivering can raise the metabolic rate to prevent hypothermia if nutritional reserves and insulation are adequate; prevention mostly depends on insulating clothing and shelter.

source.title: Dow et al. 2019, Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update (Wilderness Environ Med 30(4S), S47–S69)

facts.claim: A climber who shivers with a core still over 35 °C is cold-stressed, not hypothermic: one who shivers but looks after themselves well is unlikely to be hypothermic.

versions.note: A shivering patient with a core temperature >35 °C is cold-stressed, but not hypothermic. Section: Some patients are cold, but not hypothermic.

source.title: Dow et al. 2019, Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update (Wilderness Environ Med 30(4S), S47–S69)

facts.claim: A windproof layer protects a cold climber a great deal from the wind's loss of heat.

versions.note: In windy conditions, a windproof layer, ideally a vapor barrier, provides substantial protection from convective heat loss.

source.title: Dow et al. 2019, Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update (Wilderness Environ Med 30(4S), S47–S69)

facts.claim: The coldest wind chill a climber dressed for Everest keeps their heat in on the move (#272): about the summit's on a summit night, which climbers climb through for hours, working, in their down suits.
The coldest wind chill a climber dressed for Everest keeps their heat in at rest, standing or sitting out of a tent (#272): shivering's heat alone, cold-stressed at a moderate risk, not hypothermic.

How fast a dressed climber's core cools, in °C an hour, for each degree of wind chill colder than they keep their heat in (#272): at rest in a storm's wind chill of −45 °C, mildly hypothermic in four hours and unable to go on in ten, more slowly than the safe rewarming rate brings them back.
How much warmer a tent's air is than the air outside, out of the wind, with its climbers in it (#272).
How many times slower than bare skin a climber's face freezes behind a hood, goggles and a buff, the cheeks and nose still partly bare (#272).

How many times slower than bare skin a climber's fingers freeze in mittens that come off to clip in and work the jumar (#272): slow enough that a summit night, hours in a wind chill of −46 to −50 °C, frostnips their fingers rather than frostbiting them.
A part goes numb, white and cold, once this share of the time bare skin takes to freeze in the chill has passed (#272): numbness comes before the skin freezes.
A part is frostnipped once the time bare skin takes to freeze in the chill has passed, this many times over (#272): the first, superficial freezing, which thaws.
A part is frostbitten once the time bare skin takes to freeze in the chill has passed this many times over (#272): frozen past frostnip, and it stays.
How many hours a frostnipped part takes to thaw out of the freezing chill (#272): about the half hour a frozen part is rewarmed in.
How sure-footed a mildly hypothermic climber still is, against a warm one (#272): their movement impaired.
How fast a mildly hypothermic climber still goes, against a warm one (#272): clumsy and slower.
